DM1: every PDF method on a 1:3, covariate-re-randomised split

Replication in split_1to3/ of the all-methods analysis with a new split (25% test per arm; test:train = 1:3). The earlier analyses are untouched. Simulated data.

Bottom line
  1. New split: stratified on outcome quartiles, then re-randomised on baseline covariates (first of 5000 stratified draws in the best 2% by Mahalanobis distance). Worst covariate imbalance is 0.21–0.27 SD (random 1:3 splits: median 0.35 SD; old 80/20 split: 0.30–0.45 SD on the same features). Train/test n = Mex 120/41, Oli 127/43, Tid 126/43.
  2. All PDF methods were run (10 covariate-track, 7 ML-track, plus tuning, permutation importance, SHAP) for the continuous outcome and the responder label in each arm; every method has its code, CV and test results, and prediction plots/tables below.
  3. Covariate and ML models are parallel alternatives, not a pipeline (section 3). They share only the data, split, folds and metrics.
  4. Results (sections 4-8) are in the tables below; robustness against the old split is in section 9.

1. The 1:3 re-randomised split

Procedure (fixed before looking at any model; the test outcomes are never used except to build 4 outcome-quantile strata, as the PDF suggests for continuous outcomes): per arm, draw K=5000 candidate splits with train_test_split(test_size=0.25, stratify=outcome quartile, random_state=seed); score each by the Mahalanobis distance M between train and test covariate means; accept candidates in the best 2% of M; use the first accepted seed (Morgan & Rubin re-randomisation, so the split stays random among balanced ones). Seed, M and the candidate list are in results/split_candidates.csv.

arm split max_abs_SMD n_features_p_lt_05 outcome_SMD outcome_KS_p responder_share_diff

Outcome distribution and responder share stay matched (columns outcome_KS_p, responder_share_diff). Note that balance on measured traits does not guarantee balance on unmeasured ones, and re-randomisation does not remove the sampling noise of a test set of 41–43 patients.

2. Setup common to all methods

  • Features: log10 CTG, mosaicism, age at onset, disease duration, myotonia severity, muscle strength, PR interval, cognition, CK, insulin resistance, albumin (not in Mexiletine: constant), BMI + dummies; age omitted (= onset + duration). z-scored with train mean/sd only, applied unchanged to test.
  • Repeated stratified 5-fold CV (3 repeats, same folds for every method) on train; test scored once (results/test_scoreboard.csv). Cutoff for recall/precision/accuracy = Youden J on the train out-of-fold scores.
  • 'Top-4 covariates' rows (poly, piecewise, spline) choose their 4 covariates by |correlation with the target| inside each training fit, so no information from the test patients, or from the main project's older analyses, enters the new rows.
  • Metrics: RMSE, MAE, R² (relative to the test-set mean, as the PDF defines it); ROC-AUC, recall, precision, accuracy. 95% CIs: 2000 bootstrap resamples of the test patients.

3. Are covariate models and ML models parallel or dependent?

Parallel. The PDF presents them as two tracks that answer the same hackathon question ("can ML identify additional predictors and improve stratification beyond covariate modelling?"), so each track is fitted independently from the same training rows and judged on the same test patients. Neither needs the other's output. Differences in purpose: covariate models are chosen for which variables matter and how (coefficients, selection); ML models for predictive accuracy (importance is derived afterwards by permutation/SHAP).

Where they can be chained (optional, not done here to keep the comparison clean): use LASSO/stepwise to pre-select covariates and feed those to a forest or XGBoost; or use ML importance to decide which covariates deserve a GAM or spline. Several methods straddle the line (LASSO selects and predicts, GAM is interpretable and flexible). If a chain is used, the selection step must happen inside each training fold, as the 'top-4 covariates' rows do here. The only dependence in this analysis is the final comparison of what each method selected (section 6).

4. Methods: code and prediction results

Contents: [lm] [step] [subset] [pen] [poly] [piece] [bs] [ss] [gam] [pca] [logit] [tree] [rf] [svm] [knn] [xgb] [mlp] [tuning] [perm] [shap]

Shared R helpers used by every covariate method (model constructors, term extraction)
fitfun <- function(d) if (task == "reg") function(f) do.call("lm", list(f, data = d)) else function(f) do.call("glm", list(f, data = d, family = quote(binomial)))   # data embedded in call so stepAIC can refit
prd <- function(m, nd) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "response"))
rhs <- function(v) as.formula(paste(".t ~", paste(c(v, if (length(v) == 0) "1"), collapse = " + ")))
terms_of <- function(m) { co <- coef(m); co <- co[names(co) != "(Intercept)"]; co }

curvesel <- function(d, k = 4) cont[order(-abs(sapply(cont, function(v) cor(d[[v]], d$.t))))[seq_len(k)]]   # curve covariates chosen INSIDE each fit (train rows only): top-4 continuous by |cor| with the target
R driver: CV loop (stage=cv) and test fit/predict (stage=test)
safe <- function(fn, d, nd) tryCatch(fn(d, nd), error = function(e) list(pred = rep(NA_real_, nrow(nd)), terms = numeric(0), err = conditionMessage(e)))
if (stage == "cv") {
  fo <- read.csv(file.path(res, paste0("folds_", arm, ".csv")))
  for (nm in names(M)) for (r in unique(fo$rep)) for (k in sort(unique(fo$fold[fo$rep == r]))) {
    te <- fo$row[fo$rep == r & fo$fold == k] + 1; out <- safe(M[[nm]], tr[-te, ], tr[te, ])
    P[[length(P) + 1]] <- data.frame(method = nm, rep = r, row = te - 1, pred = out$pred)
} else {
  te <- mk(read.csv(file.path(res, paste0("test_", arm, ".csv")))); te$.t <- te[[yname]]

4a. Covariate-modelling track (R)

Linear / logistic regression (lm, glm) (Covariate track; R: stats::lm / glm)

Straight-line effect per covariate; the starting point. glm(binomial) for the responder label.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["lm / glm (all covariates)"]] <- function(d, nd) { f <- fitfun(d); m <- f(rhs(feats)); list(pred = prd(m, nd), terms = terms_of(m)) }

Stepwise selection: forward, backward, both (MASS::stepAIC) (Covariate track; R: MASS::stepAIC)

Adds/drops covariates by AIC (BIC variant: k=log n). Unstable by design - see selection frequencies in section 6.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
step_m <- function(dir, k = 2) function(d, nd) {
  f <- fitfun(d); full <- f(rhs(feats)); nul <- f(rhs(character(0)))
  m <- switch(dir, forward = stepAIC(nul, scope = list(lower = ~1, upper = formula(full)), direction = "forward", trace = 0, k = k),
              backward = stepAIC(full, direction = "backward", trace = 0, k = k), both = stepAIC(full, direction = "both", trace = 0, k = k))
  list(pred = prd(m, nd), terms = terms_of(m)) }
M[["Stepwise forward (AIC)"]] <- step_m("forward"); M[["Stepwise backward (AIC)"]] <- step_m("backward"); M[["Stepwise both (AIC)"]] <- step_m("both")
M[["Stepwise both (BIC)"]] <- function(d, nd) step_m("both", k = log(nrow(d)))(d, nd)

Best subset selection (leaps::regsubsets) (Covariate track; R: leaps::regsubsets)

Exhaustive search over all subsets up to 10 covariates, best by BIC. Continuous outcome only (leaps has no logistic version).

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
if (task == "reg") M[["Best subset (leaps, BIC, nvmax=10)"]] <- function(d, nd) {
  X <- d[feats]; rs <- regsubsets(x = as.matrix(X), y = d$.t, nvmax = 10, really.big = TRUE, method = "exhaustive"); s <- summary(rs); id <- which.min(s$bic)
  co <- coef(rs, id); xn <- cbind(1, as.matrix(nd[names(co)[-1]])); list(pred = as.numeric(xn %*% co), terms = co[-1]) }

Ridge, LASSO, elastic net (glmnet) (Covariate track; R: glmnet::cv.glmnet)

Penalised regression; lambda by 10-fold CV (lambda.min, plus the 1-SE LASSO). Same code for both outcome types (family argument).

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
gn <- function(alpha, s = "lambda.min") function(d, nd) {
  set.seed(1); X <- as.matrix(d[feats]); cvm <- cv.glmnet(X, d$.t, alpha = alpha, family = if (task == "reg") "gaussian" else "binomial", nfolds = 10)
  p <- as.numeric(predict(cvm, as.matrix(nd[feats]), s = s, type = "response")); cf <- as.matrix(coef(cvm, s = s))[-1, 1]; list(pred = p, terms = cf[cf != 0]) }
M[["Ridge (glmnet)"]] <- gn(0); M[["LASSO (glmnet, lambda.min)"]] <- gn(1); M[["LASSO (glmnet, lambda.1se)"]] <- gn(1, "lambda.1se"); M[["Elastic net (glmnet, alpha=.5)"]] <- gn(0.5)

Polynomial regression (poly, degree 2) (Covariate track; R: stats::poly)

Curved effects on the arm's 4 most outcome-correlated covariates (chosen inside every training fit, so no leakage).

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["Polynomial deg-2 (top-4 covariates)"]] <- function(d, nd) { cv_ <- curvesel(d); f <- fitfun(d); m <- f(as.formula(paste(".t ~", paste(sprintf("poly(%s, 2)", cv_), collapse = " + ")))); list(pred = prd(m, nd), terms = terms_of(m)) }

Piecewise model (cut at train tertiles) (Covariate track; R: stats::cut)

Step function per covariate; cut points are train-tertiles, re-used unchanged on new patients.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["Piecewise: cut() tertile bins (top-4 covariates)"]] <- function(d, nd) {
  cv_ <- curvesel(d); f <- fitfun(d); br <- lapply(cv_, function(v) c(-Inf, quantile(d[[v]], c(1/3, 2/3)), Inf)); names(br) <- cv_
  cutd <- function(x) { for (v in cv_) x[[paste0(v, "_bin")]] <- cut(x[[v]], br[[v]]); x }
  dd <- cutd(d); nn <- cutd(nd); m <- fitfun(dd)(as.formula(paste(".t ~", paste(paste0(cv_, "_bin"), collapse = " + ")))); list(pred = prd(m, nn), terms = terms_of(m)) }

Cubic B-splines per covariate (4 df); knots from the training rows.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["Regression spline bs(df=4) (top-4 covariates)"]] <- function(d, nd) { cv_ <- curvesel(d); f <- fitfun(d); m <- f(as.formula(paste(".t ~", paste(sprintf("bs(%s, df=4)", cv_), collapse = " + ")))); list(pred = prd(m, nd), terms = terms_of(m)) }

Smoothing spline (smooth.spline, cv=TRUE) (Covariate track; R: stats::smooth.spline)

Univariate by construction: fitted to the single strongest covariate; shows what one smooth curve can do.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["Smoothing spline (top-1 covariate, cv=TRUE)"]] <- function(d, nd) {
  cr <- abs(sapply(cont, function(v) cor(d[[v]], d$.t))); v <- cont[which.max(cr)]; ss <- smooth.spline(d[[v]], d$.t, cv = TRUE)
  p <- predict(ss, nd[[v]])$y; if (task == "bin") p <- pmin(pmax(p, 0), 1); list(pred = as.numeric(p), terms = setNames(ss$df, v)) }

Generalised additive model (mgcv::gam) (Covariate track; R: mgcv::gam)

Penalised smooth s(x,k=5) for every continuous covariate + linear dummies; REML with automatic term removal.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["GAM (mgcv, s(k=5), REML, select)"]] <- function(d, nd) {
  fr <- as.formula(paste(".t ~", paste(c(sprintf("s(%s, k=5)", cont), dums), collapse = " + "))); m <- gam(fr, data = d, family = fam, method = "REML", select = TRUE)
  st <- summary(m)$s.table; sel <- rownames(st)[st[, ncol(st)] < 0.05]; list(pred = as.numeric(predict(m, nd, type = "response")), terms = setNames(rep(1, length(sel)), gsub("^s\\(|\\)$", "", sel))) }

PCA and principal-component regression (prcomp) (Covariate track; R: stats::prcomp)

Unsupervised summary of correlated covariates (figures in section 7); PCR regresses the outcome on the first k components, k by 5-fold CV.

Code that ran (R; shared helpers in section 5)
M[["PCR (prcomp, k by 5-fold CV)"]] <- function(d, nd) {
  pc <- prcomp(d[feats], center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE); S <- pc$x; set.seed(1); idx <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(d))); kmax <- min(12, ncol(S))
  err <- sapply(1:kmax, function(k) mean(sapply(1:5, function(i) { dd <- data.frame(.t = d$.t[idx != i], S[idx != i, 1:k, drop = FALSE]); mm <- if (task == "reg") lm(.t ~ ., dd) else glm(.t ~ ., dd, family = binomial)
    p <- predict(mm, data.frame(S[idx == i, 1:k, drop = FALSE]), type = "response"); mean((d$.t[idx == i] - p)^2) })))
  k <- which.min(err); dd <- data.frame(.t = d$.t, S[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]); mm <- if (task == "reg") lm(.t ~ ., dd) else glm(.t ~ ., dd, family = binomial)
  Sn <- predict(pc, nd[feats]); list(pred = as.numeric(predict(mm, data.frame(Sn[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]), type = "response")), terms = setNames(rep(1, k), paste0("PC", 1:k))) }

4b. Machine-learning track (Python)

Shared Python helpers
def variants(task):
    out = []
    for r in registry(task):
        from sklearn.base import clone
        out.append((f"{r['name']} (untuned)", (lambda r=r: clone(r["est"])), False, r))
        cv = KFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0) if task == "reg" else StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
        out.append((f"{r['name']} (tuned, GridSearchCV)", (lambda r=r, cv=cv: GridSearchCV(clone(r["est"]), r["grid"], scoring=r["scoring"], cv=cv, n_jobs=1)), True, r))
    return out

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
nm, build, tuned, r = variants(task)[vi]; m = build().fit(Z.iloc[tr_rows], y[tr_rows]); p = predict(m, Z.iloc[te_rows], task)
sc = r["scoring"]; pi = permutation_importance(m, Z.iloc[te_rows], y[te_rows], n_repeats=5, scoring=sc, random_state=0).importances_mean

5. Supporting methods

Hyper-parameter tuning (GridSearchCV)

Every ML model appears twice: untuned (settings from the PDF snippets) and tuned (coarse grid, inner 3-fold CV on the training rows only; scoring = neg-RMSE or ROC-AUC). Selected parameters per arm are in ts.best_params (test table CSV).

Code
def variants(task):
    out = []
    for r in registry(task):
        from sklearn.base import clone
        out.append((f"{r['name']} (untuned)", (lambda r=r: clone(r["est"])), False, r))
        cv = KFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0) if task == "reg" else StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
        out.append((f"{r['name']} (tuned, GridSearchCV)", (lambda r=r, cv=cv: GridSearchCV(clone(r["est"]), r["grid"], scoring=r["scoring"], cv=cv, n_jobs=1)), True, r))
    return out

# fit inside every outer CV fold (and once on the full train for test scoring):
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
nm, build, tuned, r = variants(task)[vi]; m = build().fit(Z.iloc[tr_rows], y[tr_rows]); p = predict(m, Z.iloc[te_rows], task)
sc = r["scoring"]; pi = permutation_importance(m, Z.iloc[te_rows], y[te_rows], n_repeats=5, scoring=sc, random_state=0).importances_mean

  • Oligonucleotide: reg - log_ctg 16/16, disease_duration 9/16, family_history_Yes 7/16; bin - log_ctg 14/16, disease_duration 10/16, muscle_strength 7/16
  • Tideglusib: reg - cognitive_function 16/16, disease_duration 6/16, muscle_strength 3/16; bin - cognitive_function 16/16, family_history_Yes 4/16, ck_level 3/16

10. Caveats

  • Test sets are 41–43 patients per arm: gaps below the bootstrap CIs are not evidence of a better method.
  • Not an independent confirmation of the main project. The same 500 patients are used; the new test patients partly belonged to the old train set and the old test outcomes were seen earlier. Methods here are generic and no choice was tuned to old results, but treat this as a robustness check of the split, not new data.
  • Re-randomisation chose the split on covariates only; this does not make the resulting test metric optimistic, but it makes the test set more representative on the measured traits than a single random draw.
  • Importance (permutation, SHAP) explains models, not biology; correlated covariates (CTG vs myotonia severity) share credit.
  • Best subset is continuous-outcome only; logistic regression is classification only; the smoothing spline is univariate.
